headline: A Virginia senator, 82, is charged over a marijuana ring.
summary: Federal prosecutors arrested L. Louise Lucas, a Democrat in Virginia's Senate since 1992. She and six others, her family among them, are charged with racketeering, selling marijuana, laundering money and using her office to help the business. Her lawyer says she will plead not guilty; she calls it political. Early voting is under way.
cover_answer: Sold pot against the rules, prosecutors say. She says no.
table_question: If someone breaks a rule, does it matter when they get caught?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: A lawmaker in Virginia named Louise Lucas, who is 82, was arrested today. The government says she and her family sold a drug called marijuana in ways the law doesn't allow, and that she used her job to help them. She says she did nothing wrong. Now a judge and a jury decide, the way a referee decides a close call, and that is their job, not yours.
5-7.why: Arrested, says she didn't, a referee decides. Only if they hear her name.
5-7.why_long: A child this age takes one vivid feature for the whole event, here an 82-year-old being arrested, so this stays in the drawer unless they hear it. If they do, the script hands them a fair process: an accusation, a denial and a referee who has not called it yet. Expect "did she do it?" Nobody knows. That is what a trial is for.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: Louise Lucas, a Virginia state senator since 1992, owns a marijuana shop. Prosecutors say the family sold the drug illegally, hid the money and used her job to help it; she says not guilty. Virginia allows a little but tightly limits selling, so the fight is which side of the rulebook her shop sat on.
8-12.why: Shop, rulebook, charges, timing. Fairness pulls both ways here.
8-12.why_long: At this age a child is working out rules and whether adults apply them evenly, and this story pulls both ways: a lawmaker accused of using her job for her family, and a prosecutor moving just before an election, when the habit was to wait. The rulebook, holding versus selling, is the mechanism. Expect "is she guilty?" Nobody knows.

13-17.script: When the Justice Department charges a politician twelve days before a vote, how do you read it? Louise Lucas, 82, is charged with running a marijuana racket with her family; she says it is politics and will plead not guilty. Second: what would it take to believe the charges anyway?
13-17.why: The charge and the timing. Both can be true; ask what would settle it.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: a senator may have broken the law, and the prosecutors may have picked the moment for politics. The script asks them to keep both and say what would move them; Kuhn's point is that arguing is practised, not won by picking a side. Expect "so is it a setup?" The FBI raided her office in May.

5-7.a: The government says she sold a drug called marijuana against the rules and used her job to help her family. She says she didn't. A court decides.

8-12.a: Holding a little is. Selling is tightly limited. That's the fight.

8-12.q: Why does it matter that it's before an election?
8-12.a: Prosecutors usually wait till after a vote. The governor objected.

13-17.a: She says so, and the governor faults the timing. The FBI raid was in May.
Running an ongoing criminal operation. Prosecutors say the shop was one.
